# Part A — Logistic regression {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## 6.1 Route A — the link function

Model the log-odds as linear:

$$\log\frac{p(x)}{1-p(x)} = x^\top\beta \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
p(x) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-x^\top\beta}} = \sigma(x^\top\beta)$$

::: {.check}
The logistic function satisfies $\sigma'(z) = \sigma(z)(1-\sigma(z))$ — an identity we use
repeatedly today.
:::

## 6.1 Route B — a latent variable

Suppose an unobserved index $y_i^* = x_i^\top\beta - u_i$ with $y_i = \mathbb{1}\{y_i^* > 0\}$.

::: {.tight}
- $u_i$ standard **logistic** → $P(y_i = 1\mid x_i) = \sigma(x_i^\top\beta)$ exactly
- $u_i$ standard **normal** → probit
:::

::: {.muted}
Route B is the economist's route: $y^*$ is a latent utility difference, and the model is a random
utility model. The logit/probit choice is a choice about the distribution of unobserved
heterogeneity — and in practice the two give nearly identical fitted probabilities.
:::

## 6.2 The likelihood

$$\ell(\beta) = \sum_{i=1}^n \Big[ y_i x_i^\top\beta - \log\big(1 + e^{x_i^\top\beta}\big) \Big]$$

**Score**, using $\sigma' = \sigma(1-\sigma)$:

$$\nabla \ell(\beta) = \sum_i \big(y_i - p(x_i)\big)x_i = X^\top (y - p)$$

## Read the score

> At the optimum, the residual $y - p$ is **orthogonal to every regressor**.

::: {.check}
Exactly the OLS condition from Session 02, with fitted *probabilities* in place of fitted values.
:::

## 6.2 The Hessian, and concavity

$$\nabla^2\ell(\beta) = -\sum_i p_i(1-p_i)\,x_i x_i^\top = -X^\top W X$$

$$W = \mathrm{diag}\big(p_i(1-p_i)\big)$$

Since $W \succeq 0$, we have $-X^\top W X \preceq 0$:

::: {.check}
**The log-likelihood is concave.** Any stationary point is a global maximum. There are no local
optima.
:::

## 6.3 Newton–Raphson is IRLS

The Newton step $\beta^{(t+1)} = \beta^{(t)} + (X^\top W X)^{-1}X^\top(y-p)$ rearranges to

$$\beta^{(t+1)} = (X^\top W X)^{-1} X^\top W z, \qquad z = X\beta^{(t)} + W^{-1}(y - p)$$

which is exactly **weighted least squares** of the *adjusted response* $z$ on $X$ with weights $W$.

## Two consequences

::: {.tight}
- You reuse **all** the linear algebra of Session 02
- The asymptotic covariance is
  $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat\beta) = (X^\top W X)^{-1}$ — the inverse observed information
:::

## Perfect separation

If a hyperplane separates the classes exactly, the likelihood increases without bound as
$\|\beta\| \to \infty$: **the MLE does not exist.**

::: {.warn}
Symptoms: enormous coefficients with enormous standard errors. More common with small samples and
many dummies than students expect.
:::

::: {.muted}
Hold that thought — Part B disposes of it in one line.
:::

## 6.4 Three quantities, three uses

| Quantity | Formula | Use it when |
|---|---|---|
| Log-odds change | $\beta_j$ | Reporting the raw model |
| Odds ratio | $e^{\beta_j}$ | A clinical or credit audience |
| Marginal effect at $x$ | $\beta_j\, p(x)(1-p(x))$ | You need a probability change |
| **Average marginal effect** | $\frac1n\sum_i \beta_j\, p_i(1-p_i)$ | **Reporting to economists** |

## Why the average marginal effect

The same $\beta_j$ implies a large probability change near $p=0.5$ and almost none near $p=0.01$.

::: {.warn}
**Report average marginal effects** unless you have a reason not to. A bare odds ratio invites
misreading.
:::

## Aside — more than two classes

$$P(y=k\mid x) = \frac{e^{x^\top\beta_k}}{\sum_\ell e^{x^\top\beta_\ell}}$$

Parameters are identified only up to adding a constant vector to every $\beta_k$ — hence the
convention $\beta_K = 0$. The likelihood is again concave.

::: {.muted}
Multinomial logit imposes **independence of irrelevant alternatives** — which matters greatly for
discrete-choice work and much less for pure classification.
:::

## 6.5 A model, then a decision

A model produces $\hat p_i$. A **decision** requires a threshold $\tau$.

::: {.warn}
These are separate acts, and conflating them is the most common applied error in this session.
:::

| | Predicted 1 | Predicted 0 |
|---|---|---|
| **Actual 1** | TP | FN |
| **Actual 0** | FP | TN |

$$\text{Precision} = \frac{TP}{TP+FP}, \quad \text{Recall} = \frac{TP}{TP+FN}, \quad
\text{FPR} = \frac{FP}{FP+TN}$$

## ROC and its vice

**ROC** plots TPR against FPR as $\tau$ sweeps $[0,1]$; **AUC** equals
$P(\hat p_{\text{positive}} > \hat p_{\text{negative}})$ for a random pair.

::: {.tight}
- Threshold-free and invariant to class balance — a **virtue** for comparing models
- A **vice** for judging usefulness under heavy imbalance
:::

::: {.check}
With 2% positives, prefer the **precision–recall curve** and average precision.
:::

## Choosing $\tau$ from costs

If a false negative costs $c_{FN}$ and a false positive $c_{FP}$:

$$\boxed{\;\tau^\star = \frac{c_{FP}}{c_{FP} + c_{FN}}\;}$$

For German Credit's stated **5:1** ratio, $\tau^\star = 1/6 \approx 0.167$, not 0.5.

::: {.warn}
**The default threshold in every software package is a modelling assumption about costs that almost
nobody states out loud.**
:::

## Calibration

A model is calibrated if, among cases where $\hat p \approx 0.3$, about 30% are positive.

::: {.check}
Discrimination (AUC) and calibration are **different properties**. A model can rank perfectly and
still be badly miscalibrated.
:::

::: {.muted}
Plot a reliability diagram whenever the probability itself enters a decision.
:::

# Part B — Adding the penalty {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## 6.6 The composition

Combine Session 05's penalty with the likelihood:

$$\hat\beta = \arg\min_\beta \left\{ -\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}\Big[ y_i x_i^\top\beta - \log(1+e^{x_i^\top\beta})\Big]
+ \lambda\Big[\alpha\|\beta\|_1 + \tfrac{1-\alpha}{2}\|\beta\|_2^2\Big] \right\}$$

::: {.check}
The negative log-likelihood is convex (6.2) and both penalties are convex, so the objective is
convex. For $\alpha < 1$ it is **strictly** convex and the minimiser is unique.
:::

## The penalty cures separation

The likelihood's drive toward $\|\beta\|\to\infty$ is dominated by the penalty's growth, so a
**finite minimiser always exists**.

::: {.check}
Regularisation is here a *regularity* device, not merely a variance-reduction device.
:::

::: {.muted}
Firth's bias-reduced logistic regression is an alternative. Dropping the offending variable, once
you recognise it as a proxy for the outcome, is usually the honest answer.
:::

## 6.7 Two nested loops

**Outer.** At the current $\tilde\beta$, take the second-order Taylor expansion of the
log-likelihood. By 6.3 this *is* a weighted least-squares problem, with

$$w_i = \tilde p_i(1-\tilde p_i), \qquad z_i = x_i^\top\tilde\beta + (y_i - \tilde p_i)/w_i$$

## The inner loop

Coordinate descent — the Session 05 formula with weights inserted:

$$\beta_j \leftarrow \frac{S_{\lambda\alpha}\big(\frac1n\sum_i w_i x_{ij}(z_i - \tilde y_i^{(-j)})\big)}
{\frac1n\sum_i w_i x_{ij}^2 + \lambda(1-\alpha)}$$

with $S_\lambda(\rho) = \mathrm{sign}(\rho)(|\rho|-\lambda)_+$, the soft-thresholding
operator you derived in Session 05. Iterate, recompute weights, repeat.

## Three practical points

::: {.tight}
1. **Warm starts** down a decreasing $\lambda$ grid make the whole path cost little more than one fit.
2. An **active set** strategy cycles only over currently non-zero coefficients, checking the full set
   occasionally via the KKT conditions.
3. **Clamp $w_i$ away from zero** (e.g. at $10^{-5}$) or $z_i$ explodes for well-classified points.
:::

::: {.warn}
That third one is the bug you will hit in the practice session.
:::

## 6.8 Imbalance — three distinct interventions

| Intervention | What it changes | Effect on calibration |
|---|---|---|
| **Resampling** (SMOTE, over/under) | the empirical distribution | **Destroys** it — $\hat p$ estimates the resampled prior |
| **Class weights** in the loss | the objective | Distorts it similarly; equivalent to a prior shift |
| **Threshold adjustment** | only the decision rule | **Preserves** it completely |

## The recommendation

> Fit an **unweighted**, well-regularised model, verify **calibration**, then move the **threshold**
> using $\tau^\star$ from 6.5.

::: {.check}
You keep an interpretable probability *and* an optimal decision. Unambiguous for most economic
applications.
:::

## If you must resample, undo it

With training positive rate $\pi'$ and population rate $\pi$, correct the intercept:

$$\beta_0 \leftarrow \beta_0 - \log\!\left(\frac{\pi'}{1-\pi'}\cdot\frac{1-\pi}{\pi}\right)$$

::: {.muted}
Very few practitioners do this. Be one who does.
:::

## On SMOTE

::: {.warn}
It interpolates between minority neighbours, so synthetic points lie in the **convex hull** of
observed minority cases. With correlated financial ratios in high dimensions, those interpolants
can be economically impossible firms.
:::

::: {.muted}
Treat with scepticism.
:::

## 6.9 Selection stability

When $p \gg n$ with correlated predictors, the selected variable set is a **high-variance object** —
you saw this for the lasso in Session 05; it is worse here.

::: {.tight}
- **Stability selection** (Meinshausen & Bühlmann): many subsamples of size $n/2$, retain variables
  selected in at least $\pi_{\text{thr}}$ (e.g. 0.6) of them. Comes with a bound on the expected
  number of false selections.
- **Bootstrap selection frequencies:** simpler, and enough for a report.
:::

## How to write it up

::: {.warn}
**Never:** *"the model identified X, Y and Z as the drivers of bankruptcy."*
:::

::: {.check}
Report the selected set **with its selection frequencies**, and say that a different sample would
plausibly have produced a different list.
:::

# The practice {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## What you do

::: {.tight}
1. Fit penalised logistic on your project under grouped CV; report the base rate first
2. Produce a reliability diagram — is $\hat p$ usable as a probability?
3. State a cost ratio, derive $\tau^\star$, and report precision and recall **there**
4. Bootstrap the selection and report frequencies
:::

::: {.warn}
Report the **base rate** before any accuracy figure, so it can be read against something.
:::

## The two-minute report

::: {.tight}
1. **What I did** — the model, the CV scheme, the cost ratio you assumed
2. **The number** — performance at *your* threshold, not the best over all thresholds
3. **The catch** — calibration, and the instability of the selected set
:::

Full brief: [`02-practice/README.md`](02-practice/README.md)
:::
